dc.title: Reversal of the Desertification Process in Susceptible Areas of Brazil: Sustainable Agroforestry Practices and Biodiversity Conservation (REDESER) - GCP/BRA/085/GFF
dc.contributor.author: FAO;
dc.description.abstract: The project promoted sustainable management of land and natural resources in the Caatinga biome through field demonstrations, institutional strengthening and knowledge generation. The REDESER project supported communities and local institutions in adopting production practices adapted to the semi-arid context, including agroforestry systems, SFM and the restoration of degraded landscapes.Through partnerships with civil society organizations, universities and public agencies, the project strengthened technical capacities and supported the development of territorial planning instruments such as Integrated Natural Resource Management (INRM) plans. It also fostered knowledge exchange among farmers and technicians through training activities, demonstration units and community exchanges.At the same time, the REDESER project worked to strengthen coordination between local experiences and national public policies related to combating desertification, restoration of degraded areas and sustainable rural development. The project also emphasized inclusive participation, encouraging the involvement and leadership of women and young people in sustainable production systems and community-based natural resource management.

Coastal hazards and adaptation in Small Island Developing States based on the Coastal Hazard Wheel framework
Rosendahl Appelquist, L.; Hendriksen, G.; Micha, I.; Dees, N.; Alves, B.;
https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/ce2139en
2026-11-05T18:09:20Z
2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
dc.title: Coastal hazards and adaptation in Small Island Developing States based on the Coastal Hazard Wheel framework
dc.contributor.author: Rosendahl Appelquist, L.; Hendriksen, G.; Micha, I.; Dees, N.; Alves, B.;
dc.description.abstract: Coastal hazards pose interconnected challenges for Small Island Developing States (SIDS), where people,infrastructure and economic activities are exposed to changing coastal conditions. Understanding thesechallenges is essential for planning adaptation measures that respond to national circumstances andlocal needs. This technical brief forms part of a series covering 40 SIDS and brings together informationon coastal characteristics, climate-related hazards, and the exposure of communities and assets. It offerspolicymakers, planners, and environmental stakeholders an accessible basis for identifying adaptationpriorities and considering where interventions may be most relevant.The brief examines the country’s predominant coastal types and assesses five main hazards under projectedclimate change: ecosystem disruption, gradual inundation, saltwater intrusion, erosion and flooding. Nationalmaps illustrate the distribution of these hazards, while estimates of the population living in hazard-proneareas and the value of exposed assets help clarify their potential societal and economic implications. Drawingthese elements together, the brief highlights relevant adaptation interventions and connects the assessmentof coastal conditions with practical considerations for managing risk at local, regional and national levels.The analysis uses the Coastal Hazard Wheel, a universal coastal classification and management frameworkdesigned to guide adaptation and support communication about coastal challenges worldwide. Its consistentapproach provides a common basis for understanding different coastal settings and considering appropriateresponses. Within the wider series, this brief also contributes to a broader assessment of the adaptationchallenges facing SIDS. By linking national evidence with a shared framework, the series supports dialogueamong national and international stakeholders and helps inform decisions on coastal adaptation.
2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
Coastal hazards and adaptation in Small Island Developing States based on the Coastal Hazard Wheel framework
Rosendahl Appelquist, L.; Hendriksen, G.; Micha, I.; Dees, N.; Alves, B.;
https://openknowledge.fao.org/handle/20.500.14283/ce2092en
2026-11-05T18:27:53Z
2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
dc.title: Coastal hazards and adaptation in Small Island Developing States based on the Coastal Hazard Wheel framework
dc.contributor.author: Rosendahl Appelquist, L.; Hendriksen, G.; Micha, I.; Dees, N.; Alves, B.;
dc.description.abstract: This brief is part of a series of technical briefs on coastal hazards and adaptation for 40 Small Island Developing States (SIDS). It aims to provide a broad overview of national coastal conditions, hazard presence, human and societal exposure, and relevant focus areas for adaptation interventions. It provides detailed information on the most prevalent coastal types, the presence of the five main hazard types of ecosystem disruption, gradual inundation, saltwater intrusion, erosion and flooding under the projected climate change, the share of the national population living in hazard-prone areas and the value of assets exposed to coastal hazards. This is coupled with national hazard mapping for the five main hazard types and recommendations on relevant adaptation interventions to address the hazards.The brief builds on the Coastal Hazard Wheel framework that is a universal coastal classification and management system developed to guide coastal adaptation efforts and facilitate coastal communication worldwide. The overview is aimed at national and international policymakers, planners and environmental stakeholders and should provide a systemic understanding of coastal conditions, challenges and relevant adaptation actions at local, regional and national level. Furthermore, it should contribute to an understanding of the challenges to the world’s SIDS as part of a broader adaptation assessment.
2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
